topComments.author: patryk_builds
topComments.text: The most useful line on the page for operators is easy to miss: after updating, `nginx -s reload` does not load the new binary, you need a restart. I'd expect a fair number of hosts to be "patched" on disk and still running the old worker for weeks. The other one is the caveat about version strings. Distro packages and container images backport fixes without changing the version, so `nginx -v` can't confirm exposure or safety by itself. For anyone pinning an image tag like nginx:1.27-alpine, the question is whether that tag was rebuilt, and the only way to know is to pull again and compare digests. On the 98.9% figure: the page is careful to call it version prevalence, which I appreciate. But the fourth condition in your checklist, external h2 negotiation, is measurable from outside with an ALPN probe. Did you run that against the same Shodan set? The share of affected-version hosts that actually negotiate h2 on a public port would be a much better estimate of real exposure. I checked my own small server after reading this and it turned out not to matter, since the proxy in front is Caddy. What it did show me is that I couldn't have answered "which proxy, which version, is h2 on" from memory, and that's probably the common case for small deployments.

[Note 1 : Indirection through a pointer to an incomplete type (other than cv void) is valid. The lvalue thus obtained can be used in limited ways (to initialize a reference, for example); this lvalue must not be converted to a prvalue, see 7.3.2. — end note] and null pointers as follows: Every value of pointer type is one of the following: a pointer to an object or function (the pointer is said to point to the object or function), or a pointer past the end of an object (7.6.6), or the null pointer value for that type, or an invalid pointer value. I've simplified the function and given a couple of example conditions: simulation1 <- function(states, max.steps=15) { mat <- matrix(NA, nrow=3, ncol=max.steps) mat[, 1] <- 1 for (i in seq_len(max.steps-1)+1) { mat[, i] <- sample(states, 3, rep=TRUE) if (min(mat[, i]) == max(states)) { break } } mat } set.seed(23) simulation1(1:3) simulation2 <- function(states, max.steps=15) { mat <- matrix(NA, nrow=3, ncol=max.steps) mat[, 1] <- 1 for (i in seq_len(max.steps-1)+1) { mat[, i] <- sample(states, 3, rep=TRUE) if (all(mat[, i] == mat[, i-1])) { break } } mat } set.seed(23) simulation2(1:3) So far what Ive come up with is this: simulation3 <- function(states, max.steps=15, break.cond="FALSE") { break.cond <- parse(text=break.cond) mat <- matrix(NA, nrow=3, ncol=max.steps) mat[, 1] <- 1 for (i in seq_len(max.steps-1)+1) { mat[, i] <- sample(states, 3, rep=TRUE) if (eval(break.cond)) { break } } mat } set.seed(23) simulation3(1:3) set.seed(23) simulation3(1:3, break.cond="min(mat[, i]) == max(states)") set.seed(23) simulation3(1:3, break.cond="all(mat[, i] == mat[, i-1])") It works OK, but I wonder if there are some potential issues I haven't seen? I also wonder how user friendly it is, and if there already exist some more 'canonical' way of doing this? Of course it's uncommented and undocumented, I'm thinking more of ways to make the use itself more intuitive.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How is internal silicon testing performed on SWD-only MCUs (like ATSAMC21N18A) if JTAG pins are absent?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am working with a microcontroller that features only Serial Wire Debug (SWD) support, such as the Microchip ATSAMC21N18A (ARM Cortex-M0+). However, looking at the hardware design and debug headers (such as the standard 10-pin Cortex debug connector layout), footprints often include pads or pins for traditional JTAG signals ( TCK , TDI , TMS , TDO ). Since code flashing and debugging on these ICs take place exclusively over the 2-wire SWD interface ( SWCLK and SWDIO ), I am trying to understand how internal testing works: If the MCU itself only exposes SWD, how are all the internal blocks (such as ADCs, internal flash, RAM, and CAN-FD controllers) tested during manufacturing or IC characterization? How is the internal JTAG block or boundary scan connected or bypassed inside the silicon when full JTAG pins are not brought out to the package or used externally? Any explanation of how foundry-level Automated Test Equipment (ATE) or internal test logic handles this would be greatly appreciated!

stackOverflowQuestions.title: iOS 27: bars don't follow vertical ScrollViews inside a horizontal paging ScrollView (hairline at rest, no soft edge)
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I have a screen that pages horizontally between questions. Each page has its own vertical ScrollView . On iOS 27 the navigation bar and bottom toolbar don't behave as they do for a plain ScrollView : Top bar: it shows its scroll edge effect (a tinted band with a hairline) at rest, with nothing scrolled underneath. Bottom toolbar: the .soft style set on the page never appears. The same page on its own, outside the pager, behaves correctly: the bars are clear at rest, the standard top effect appears when the text scrolls under the navigation bar, and the soft effect appears at the bottom. Minimal example New iOS App (SwiftUI) project, deployment target iOS 27: import SwiftUI @main struct PagerEdgeEffectApp: App { var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { NavigationStack { List { NavigationLink("Single scroll view (expected)") { SingleScreen() } NavigationLink("Paged scroll views (problem)") { PagerScreen() } } .navigationTitle("Edge Effects") } } } } struct LongPage: View { let number: Int var body: some View { ScrollView { Text(String(repeating: "Page \(number). The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
